item.title: The Frenzy Behind Getting an Initiative on the California Ballot
item.description:
Dederek Huff scanned the grassy hillside of Dolores Park in San Francisco one day this spring and saw dozens of people relaxing on picnic blankets and park benches.

To most people, it was an idyllic scene on a sunny day. To Mr. Huff, however, it was an opportunity to earn as much as $125 from each person in the park who would sign the stack of petitions under his arm.

“How y’all doing?” Mr. Huff asked as he approached a group of friends on a blanket. “Are you registered to vote?”

With his ease talking to strangers and his knack for reading a crowd, Mr. Huff used the same skills he said he had developed in a very different setting: selling party drugs on the Las Vegas Strip.

He had come to San Francisco because word had spread that campaigns were paying big money to place measures on the November ballot. So much, in fact, that Mr. Huff said he found he could make more money dealing democracy than dope.

“This is better than drug money,” said Mr. Huff, who has had drug-related arrests in Nevada, records show.

Mr. Huff was part of a small army of petition circulators who fanned out to shopping centers and street corners this spring, becoming the main reason that the ballots sent to California voters this month are stuffed with statewide initiatives.

California’s direct democracy system began over a century ago as a populist reform meant to empower citizens and bypass the special interests that controlled the State Legislature. Over the years, though, ballot measures have morphed into a sprawling industry fueled by moneyed interests that spend whatever it takes to put their ideas before voters.

This year, campaigns had to collect nearly 900,000 valid signatures to qualify a measure for the November ballot. To hit that number, most initiative efforts had to hire companies that specialize in this slice of the political process. The firms, in turn, contracted with smaller companies that paid people like Mr. Huff for each verified signature.

A flurry of spending was set off in January when a health care workers union began circulating petitions to put the billionaire tax on the ballot. That prompted a coalition of billionaires to flood the marketplace with three countermeasures that could void the tax initiative if they were to receive more votes in November.

Campaigns paid as much as $15 per signature, drawing a raft of enterprising workers — and some alleged fraudsters — to take part in this political underworld. It turned into a bonanza for workers like Mr. Huff, who said he made $43,000 in three months.

“That’s the most money I’ve made in three months of my life,” said Mr. Huff, 38.

All told, California ballot measure campaigns spent $126.5 million on circulating petitions during the first half of the year, four times as much as they spent in the same period in 2024, the last regular election year, according to state campaign finance reports.

As the price per signature doubled in March, a Facebook group for petition circulators lit up with excitement. Commenters called it a legendary season and punctuated their posts with money bag emojis. They shared pictures of invoices for tens of thousands of dollars as they submitted heaps of petitions. Employers recruited circulators from other parts of the country, sometimes offering housing or transportation.

But reports of bad actors and concerns of fraud also permeated the group. Workers posted warnings about managers who didn’t pay them and people who stole signed petitions. Some veteran petitioners expressed fear that the high price for signatures this year was spurring scams.

Things become so frenzied that men in ski masks handed out $5 bills and slices of pizza to people who signed petitions in a San Francisco neighborhood known for drug addiction and homelessness. And last month, three people were criminally charged after they were accused of paying people to sign petitions using stolen identities on Skid Row in Los Angeles.

In one pocket of Southern California, an experienced circulator with the biblical-sounding name of Third Corinthians Walker tried to instill some order. He confronted petition circulators who gave misleading information to voters or offered illegal giveaways. Then he posted their photos on the Facebook group and cited the laws he contended they were violating.

“This was the most hectic season I ever been in, in 25 years,” said Mr. Walker, 46, who lives in Redlands, Calif., about 60 miles east of downtown Los Angeles.

A lot of what he saw fell short of criminal behavior but broke the unspoken code of signature gathering, Mr. Walker said.

There were petitioners who set up tables at 2 a.m. to claim the best spot at a shopping center hours before stores opened. The “turf jumpers” who encroached on spots that other petitioners had already claimed. The “runners” who roamed parking lots and approached people as they got out of their cars.

Mr. Walker grew up in Kansas City, Mo. By the time he was 21, his felony record of gun and drug charges made it difficult to find employment. Feeling desperate, Mr. Walker saw a newspaper ad for a job promising $100 a day and went to an orientation on circulating petitions.

Over time, the work took him to places that he might never have otherwise seen: Florida, Nebraska, Ohio and, eventually, California.

“I felt like it was a blessing from the Lord,” Mr. Walker said.

Now, he runs his petition business with his mother, Melba Walker. They share a home in Southern California where, during the busy season, stacks of petitions covered the coffee table.

Mr. Walker likes the autonomy that comes with his profession, the ability to set his own hours and choose where he spends his time. He said he varies his pitch depending on the politics of the region. When he petitioned in a conservative area this year, he often led with the anti-tax measures; in liberal neighborhoods, he tended to start with the billionaire tax.

Now that it’s the offseason for petitioners, Mr. Walker keeps busy by playing video games and making graphic designs with Christian themes. He is also helping his mother write a book about their experiences as signature gatherers.

In San Francisco, Alex Carpenter, 49, made his first foray into petitioning this year after work dried up on the Northern California cannabis farm where he had spent the last several years.

Signature gathering appealed to Mr. Carpenter’s liberal activist streak, so he set up a table on a bustling corner near Golden Gate Park. It was close to his favorite coffee shop and had a lamppost where he could do pull-ups during lulls in foot traffic. He scrawled “Tax Billionaire$?” on a piece of card stock and taped it to the side of his table.

Many of the petitions on his clipboards represented causes Mr. Carpenter believed in. He liked the proposals to tax billionaires to fund health care, extend a tax hike on high-income earners to fund education and raise sales taxes to fund Bay Area transit. He focused on getting signatures for those initiatives.

He said he was still able to make close to $200 an hour, even though he didn’t actively pursue signatures for the highest compensated proposals that were backed by billionaires. Still, Mr. Carpenter had petitions for those measures on his table, in case voters took the time to get to the bottom of his stack of clipboards.

“I’m trying to make a living,” he said. “I would love to see them make it to the polls and fail.”

Mr. Huff, the petition circulator who sought signatures from voters in Dolores Park, also has strong political views.

He is a conservative and considers himself a part of President Trump’s MAGA movement. He has had an interest in politics ever since he was a teenager growing up in Louisville, Ky., he said.

That didn’t stop him from trying to make as much cash as possible in San Francisco, one of the nation’s most Democratic cities and where Mr. Trump is deeply unpopular.

After he finished gathering signatures this spring, Mr. Huff returned home to Las Vegas, where he spent time with his family for several weeks and used some of his petition money to buy new furniture and get work done on his teeth.

Despite his conservative views, Mr. Huff said he would do petition work for any campaign that pays him. So when a friend offered him a job gathering signatures for liberal-backed initiatives in Colorado this summer, Mr. Huff packed his bags and went.

Then he heard that conservative interest groups were also paying for signatures in Colorado.

“‘Well, bro,’ I said, ‘You got to get me on both petitions,’” Mr. Huff recalled.

“If I’m going to Colorado, I need as much petitions in my hand as possible because, of course, I’m trying to make the most money.”

Jill Cowan contributed reporting from Los Angeles. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Ken Paxton Has Tried to Overturn Tight Elections. He’s in One of His Own.
item.description:
In the immediate aftermath of the 2020 election, President Trump’s allies searched for a Republican state attorney general willing to back a last-ditch legal effort to challenge the results.

They found their man in Texas: Ken Paxton.

“No one had the courage or the clarity of legal understanding to do it,” Aaron Reitz, a top deputy to Mr. Paxton at the time, said in an interview. “Paxton and I were adamant that something needed to be done.”

The suit quickly failed at the U.S. Supreme Court, which found Texas had no standing to try to invalidate votes cast in another state. But it firmly established Mr. Paxton, the Texas attorney general, as a partisan fighter willing to wield the power of his office to aid Republicans, attack Democrats and challenge election results. It made him a conservative star and helped him secure Mr. Trump’s critical endorsement, propelling Mr. Paxton forward as the party’s nominee this year for U.S. Senate in Texas.

Early voting starts on Monday.

Since 2020, Mr. Paxton has continued to use his office to intervene in election disputes and pursue political opponents. Mr. Paxton has sued the former congressman Beto O’Rourke, tried to shut down a Latino voter registration group, opposed the counting of provisional ballots in Houston and unsuccessfully tried to criminally indict a sitting county election administrator.

Now, as he is locked in an extremely close contest against James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, Mr. Paxton’s record of election-related legal challenges and partisan legal actions has raised the question of how he would respond, in his capacity as attorney general and as a candidate, if he were to lose in November.

The Texas Senate race appears to have all the makings for a potential post-election legal fight by Mr. Paxton, should he lose. The contest is especially important to Republicans, who risk losing a statewide race for the first time in three decades and whose control of the U.S. Senate could hinge on the outcome. Current polls show Mr. Talarico with an edge in a tightening race.

“We have to win,” Mr. Paxton said at a rally hosted by President Trump in San Antonio this month.

Mr. Paxton, now in his third term as attorney general, has pushed to expand the powers of his office to prosecute criminal violations of Texas election law. Those efforts led to a clash with the state’s highest criminal court, made up of all Republican judges, which ruled that he lacked the authority under the state Constitution to independently prosecute election crimes.

After that loss, Mr. Paxton campaigned against the judges who ruled against him and were up for re-election, helping to oust them in a Republican primary in 2024. The next year, Republicans in the Texas Legislature passed a new law, Senate Bill 12, granting Mr. Paxton the authority to prosecute election crimes. But he has yet to test its constitutionality, and legal experts have said courts may again stymie Mr. Paxton if he tries.

His campaign defended his record.

“Ken Paxton has never apologized for enforcing Texas election law, and he never will,” Mr. Paxton’s campaign spokeswoman, Madison Cercy, said. “When elections are run fairly and the law is followed, every Texan wins.”

The attorney general’s office could also play a role, post-election, in investigating allegations of criminal conduct, or in securing election materials if asked by the secretary of state, who was appointed by Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican. The examination of the election materials would be directed by a state court.

Elections experts and voting security advocates said they worried that election challenges could be made in Texas, but they did not believe such challenges would be effective.

“The power he has under Texas law to enforce those criminal laws is quite limited,” said David Froomkin, a law professor at the University of Houston.

David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research in Washington, D.C., said that while the election could “potentially be a very volatile situation,” he was confident the courts and election officials in Texas were “going to hold firm.”

Mr. Abbott is tasked with certifying election results under state law, except in his own race and the lieutenant governor’s race, when the final canvass is done by the Legislature.

The role of the governor and Legislature in this process is ceremonial, election experts said, though he or the Legislature could face pressure to delay certification. This year, Mr. Abbott named Nate Schatzline, a hard-right former state representative who has questioned the 2020 election results, to be a senior adviser on elections.

Election challenges are permitted under Texas law. But Texas Republicans have, in recent years, challenged election results even when the outcome appeared clear.

In Harris County, which includes Houston, Republicans contested losses in more than a dozen races in 2022 — including one that the Democrat won by 15 points. Republicans cited what they said were problems at the polls. A court ordered a new election in only one case, a local judicial race.

Mr. Paxton also intervened on Election Day in 2022 to stop the counting of provisional ballots cast at locations in Harris County that had been kept open an extra hour. He sought to have the votes discarded. The Texas Supreme Court ruled against Mr. Paxton, ordering them to be counted — but left the possibility of further litigation open should the ballots cast during the extended voting hour swing any results. (They didn’t.)

Even within his own office, Mr. Paxton’s 2020 election challenge in support of Mr. Trump appeared to be contentious.

The solicitor general at the time, Kyle Hawkins, did not sign the Supreme Court filing, which Mr. Paxton signed himself along with Kurt Olsen, a lawyer who helped craft the unusual lawsuit that tried to challenge the election.

“Ken Paxton showed a tremendous amount of courage to take this on,” Mr. Olsen said in an interview this month.

Mr. Paxton, along with Mr. Reitz, his deputy for legal strategy, then brought the case to other Republican attorneys general to get them to file a supporting brief, Mr. Reitz said in the interview. Seventeen attorneys general signed on.

“It was a moment of character-revealing pressure,” Mr. Reitz said.

The Supreme Court quickly turned them all down.

Still, Mr. Paxton stood by his election challenge at a rally with Mr. Trump in Washington on Jan. 6, 2021. “If you look at what Georgia did, they capitulated, they consented,” Mr. Paxton told the crowd, referring to the state’s rapid certifications of its results. “We kept fighting in Texas.”

Mr. Olsen, who previously served as an elections czar for the White House, now works for the Justice Department. He recently stepped down from a high-profile elections investigation.

Mr. Reitz is now the top federal prosecutor in the Southern District of Texas, which includes Houston. He said in the interview that he would “muster all of my legal and law enforcement troops to ensure that federal law is upheld” in the 2026 election. But, he added, elections are primarily a state matter.

Since 2020, Mr. Paxton has announced dozens of election-related actions, including investigations and lawsuits.

Mr. Paxton tried in 2021 to prosecute Dana DeBeauvoir, who ran elections in Travis County, which includes Austin, on a charge of obstructing a poll observer in violation of Texas law. A grand jury declined to indict. In an interview, Ms. DeBeauvoir urged vigilance. “We’re at high alert,” she said. She added, “Let’s not let scare tactics work.”

In 2024, Mr. Paxton opened an investigation into Jolt Initiative, claiming the organization, which focuses on registering young Latino voters, had been illegally registering unauthorized migrants. The group sued, and a federal judge in Austin blocked his investigation, ruling the attorney general had acted in “bad faith.”

“Defendant could not offer any plausible proof,” the judge, Robert Pitman, wrote.

The suit had a significant financial impact, said Jackie Bastard, Jolt’s executive director, forcing it to cut its staff to five people from 35. The group has been able to register voters this year, Ms. Bastard said, but not at the same scale.

Then last fall, Mr. Paxton sued Mr. O’Rourke, the former Democratic congressman, and his voter registration group, claiming potential fund-raising violations. An all-Republican appeals court sided with Mr. O’Rourke. (The Texas Supreme Court, whose nine members are also all Republicans, declined to intervene.)

But as with Jolt, the case cost Mr. O’Rourke’s group time and more than $400,000, and, had it continued, could have bankrupted the organization, Mr. O’Rourke said at the time.

“We have seen Paxton try to use the power of the office to promote his political goals and the goals of his allies,” said Mimi Marziani, a lawyer and the former president of the Texas Civil Rights Project who represented Mr. O’Rourke.

“What I will say, which gives me a lot of hope,” she added, “is that by and large he has not been successful in the courts.”

A dispute over the election could end up before the Texas Supreme Court. The court’s newest member is Mr. Hawkins, the former solicitor general who did not sign on to Mr. Paxton’s election challenge in 2020.

item.title: Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?
item.description:
It’s triage season.

With just over two weeks to go until the midterm elections, Republicans reeling in a sour national environment have begun pulling spending out of tough territory, essentially cutting their losses in some races in an effort to rescue others.

North Carolina appears to be out. Kansas is in. Some House incumbents in New Jersey and Iowa are now on their own, while others in places like Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are receiving fresh infusions of national cash.

But even as the battleground moves into redder territory, Republicans see some signs of hope.

Polls are tightening in three Senate races in which Democrats have enjoyed narrow but consistent polling leads: Texas, Ohio and Michigan. And, thanks to a cascade of outside money, Republicans have ample resources to keep hammering their opponents in those states and beyond. Still, Democrats believe that momentum and time are on their side.

Republicans’ main super PAC has now spent or reserved more than $11.6 million shoring up Marshall, who has struggled with fund-raising in the face of a stiff challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Democratic pastor.

Those tossups still include other red states such as Alaska and Iowa. Republican groups have also spent millions in Nebraska and South Carolina in an effort to stave off any more surprising momentum from their opponents in two more states President Trump has won handily.

Another week, another set of House races shifted by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report toward Democrats. This time, it was 11 races, more than half of which are in the Midwest.

Democrats are moving ahead with plans to spend money in ever-redder battlegrounds, including House districts in states such as Colorado, South Carolina and Texas. In those districts, voters heavily favored Trump in 2024.

Republicans are sending resources to help incumbents such as Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Bryan Steil of Wisconsin.

They are also pulling back from some of their offensive plays. The Congressional Leadership Fund and a political action committee aligned with Trump’s operation have both paused their ad spending in the district held by Representative Tom Suozzi, a Long Island Democrat, according to data from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Republicans have a significant advantage in midterm spending, powered by their reliance on big donors and outside groups. That’s allowed them to spend more than $300 million more than Democrats on the Senate races that could determine control of the chamber.

There’s been lots of attention paid to the Senate race in Texas, where Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, has funneled $158 million to prop up the scandal-prone state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

But it’s actually Ohio that could be the most expensive Senate general election race of the midterms, according to AdImpact, with more than $420 million in total spending.

For the upcoming week alone, Republicans have reserved nearly $23 million in ads supporting Senator Jon Husted. Former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, has nearly $11.5 million booked.

The race appears to be a top priority for Trump, who has rallied twice in the state this month. He also held a rally in Northern Kentucky — which is part of the Cincinnati media market — over the weekend.

Graham is campaigning for a full term in the seat that her brother, Lindsey Graham, held for decades before he suddenly died in July, and she’s been deeply reliant on the support of the president.

item.title: Latest Climate Report Warns of Major Upheaval to California Way of Life
item.description:
In just a few decades, summers in California will not only be much hotter, but will also stretch for months longer. Floods will become more widespread and extreme. Exposure to wildfire smoke will kill thousands more people every year.

Those are the dire projections of California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment, a report produced by California every few years that analyzes the impacts of changing weather patterns on the nation’s most-populous state.

The future laid out in the report, which was published on Monday, touches on familiar warnings: more wildfires, bigger storms, longer droughts. But it illustrates in unsettling detail just how quickly the climate is being reshaped, and reveals what is likely to be major upheaval to long-established ways of life in California.

According to the report, average temperatures are likely to increase in California by about 4 degrees Fahrenheit by the middle of the century, and by 5 to 8 degrees by 2100. Current warming in California is unprecedented compared with the past century and estimates for the past millennium, the report shows.

More and more, warm weather will arrive in California earlier in the year and persist later, with summer conditions lasting for 135 days on average by the middle of the century, compared with an average of 90 days between 1981 and 2010, according to the report. That prolonged summer will have widespread impacts, including on fire risk, tourism, agriculture and wildlife.

The warmer conditions will also mean a 40 percent reduction by midcentury in California’s snowpack in the Sierra Nevada, which feeds the state’s reservoirs. What once fell as snow will instead fall as rain and immediately become runoff. This will lead to more severe droughts, according to the report.

Many Californians have already lived through the beginnings of these trends. The state this year logged its warmest August on record. And several of the most destructive fires in state history have happened in the last decade, including the wildfires last year in Los Angeles that were among the costliest disasters in U.S. history.

Abby Edwards, senior deputy director for the Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, which produced the assessment, said she hoped the report would alert communities and decision makers about where to focus their efforts as the climate continues to change.

The report, which weaves together existing and new, state-commissioned research, contains multiple scenarios based on different greenhouse gas emissions levels in the coming years, as well as recommendations for how to adapt to changing climate patterns.

“The future is not predetermined,” Ms. Edwards said in an interview.

The report comes as the Trump administration has been undermining California’s position as a national leader in environmental protection. As the world’s fourth-largest economy, California’s environmental regulations have influenced car and consumer goods manufacturers, and many of the state’s green policies have been adopted by other states in what’s known as the “California effect.”

Among the recent moves from the Trump administration: It ordered an oil company to restart a pipeline off Santa Barbara that caused one of the state’s largest oil spills in 2015; it announced $75 million for a new coal export terminal in Oakland that city officials have tried to stop for nearly a decade; and it has signaled that it could curb the power of the California Coastal Commission, which has been entrusted with protecting the state’s 840-mile shoreline for more than a half-century.

“As the Trump administration turns its back on science, California is doubling down on climate action, on protecting our communities, and on building a safer future,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.

The state’s assessments began in 2006 under former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger as a way to evaluate the specific threats of global warming on the state. This year’s assessment was the most extensive yet.

Beyond the statistics, the report also laid out how a changing climate could threaten beloved ways of life in California, such as skiing in the Sierra Nevada and going to the beach.

A longer summer means a shorter winter for California, and warmer temperatures are expected to blanket lower-elevation ski resorts with rain instead of snow. The snowpack is expected to fall by 60 percent by 2100.

The report also found that without major intervention, as much as three-quarters of California’s beaches could disappear — either seasonally or permanently — by 2100 because of coastal erosion. In that same time frame, sea level rise is expected to threaten $78 billion worth of property because of coastal flooding.

The state’s agricultural industry is expected to take a major hit as well.

Many crops require a certain number of hours of cold temperature to develop properly, and warmer temperatures could decrease fruit yields in some parts of the state by as much as 40 percent, according to the report.

At the same time, water shortages could mean that the number of acres that farmers irrigate could decline dramatically, including by up to 40 percent in the San Joaquin Valley, a major agricultural hub.

item.title: Trump Says Work on Disputed Golf Course Will Begin Immediately
item.description:
President Trump wrote on social media on Monday that work was “scheduled to begin IMMEDIATELY” to overhaul a Washington golf course, escalating tensions with a federal judge who has prohibited the administration from cutting trees at the site.

Mr. Trump’s post came ahead of a morning showdown in federal court over the fate of the course.

Upon learning last week that the Interior Department had cleared hundreds of trees from the course, apparently in preparation for larger changes, the judge, Ana C. Reyes, had prohibited parks officials from taking down more trees until Oct. 26. She also requested that top administration officials appear at the hearing to discuss the issue.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump announced that the course, East Potomac Golf Links, would close for a 14-month renovation on Nov. 15, before returning to social media Monday morning to castigate the judge and announce the project would move forward.

He described Judge Reyes, an appointee of President Joseph R. Biden Jr., as “a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane.” The Justice Department had requested that audio be released of a hearing she conducted last week, in which she angrily took the Trump administration to task for removing trees with minimal notice.

Ahead of the hearing on Monday, Judge Reyes also issued a forceful opinion rebuffing calls by the Justice Department that she recuse herself from the case, denying that the record in the case demonstrated bias, as the administration had alleged.

She pointed out that she had consistently rejected what she described as premature requests by the group suing that she block work at the course. Instead, she wrote that she had approached the case as a “pragmatist” who had urged the parties in July to hammer out an agreement on their own, rather than pre-emptively halt work by court order. She had instead asked the government to provide notice before undertaking major work at the course.

“Between February 13, when this case was filed, and October 11, the court had not barred the government from taking any action in East Potomac, including tree removal,” she wrote.

“It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion,” she added. “But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record. By any objective measure, the Government fails to meet the standard for recusal.”

item.title: Supreme Court to Hear New Case on Race and School Admissions
item.description:
The Supreme Court announced on Monday that it would revisit the issue of race and school admissions, three years after it sharply restricted affirmative action in higher education.

The case involves four selective public middle schools in Montgomery County, Md., just outside the nation’s capital. A group of mostly Asian American parents sued the school system after it changed its admissions criteria, saying that the new rules unconstitutionally discriminated against Asian American students.

In 2023, the Supreme Court struck down race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina. The justices did not address other school policies intended to diversify student bodies that do not explicitly address race.

Since then the court has declined to hear several other challenges to admissions criteria at elite public schools, including one from Virginia and another from the military academy at West Point.

It takes the votes of four justices to grant review, however, and several justices had previously signaled their interest in continuing to explore the implications of the court’s decision affecting higher education. In the Virginia case, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. dissented, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, saying the court should have taken the case.

The justices also agreed on Monday to hear a challenge to federal bans on home distillation of whiskey and other spirits. An Ohio engineer had brought a lawsuit against a nearly 160-year-old federal ban on home distilling, in a case that will test 1860s-era prohibitions. The two cases will be added to the justices’ calendar for oral argument next year and decided before the Supreme Court’s term ends in late June or early July.

In the admissions case, the Maryland school district adopted a new lottery system for selecting eligible fifth graders for four highly competitive magnet middle schools after the coronavirus pandemic.

To be placed in a pool of eligible students, a candidate must have received an A grade in certain subjects, performed above a fourth-grade level in reading or math and scored in the 85th percentile on a standardized test adjusted for “local norms” such as the socioeconomic status of a specific elementary school population.

Students from schools with high poverty rates, for instance, are compared to other students from high-poverty schools.

In court filings, school officials described the process as “a race-neutral, race-blind lottery” adopted after abandoning an in-person exam because of pandemic constraints.

A group of families known as the Association for Education Fairness sued, arguing the lottery unconstitutionally discriminated against Asian American students. The families told the court that Asian American students who attended a high-performing elementary school “disproportionately must obtain substantially higher” standardized test scores to be eligible for the lottery than students of other races who attend lower-performing schools.

In response, school officials noted that at two of the county’s four magnet middle schools, the proportion of Asian Americans among admitted students increased in the first year of the new admissions policy.

A district court judge in Maryland dismissed the challenge, finding no evidence that the policy was enacted with a discriminatory intent. The judge said the policy was meant to account for economic disparities across different schools — a consideration the judge said was “wholly permissible.”

“Alleged disparity in treatment based on socioeconomic status alone does not make plausible discrimination on account of race,” wrote the judge, Paula Xinis.

item.title: Republicans Attack El-Sayed’s Faith. The Candidate’s New Ad Highlights It.
item.description:
The campaign of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, is airing a new 30-second ad leaning into his Muslim faith, which has fueled many of the attacks Republicans have hurled at him in a hotly contested race.

Here’s a look at the ad.

The ad features Dr. El-Sayed sitting in a leather armchair, hands clasped around a mug and speaking soberly. As it cuts to black-and-white nature scenes and images of places of worship, the candidate describes how faith shapes his life. He never explicitly names his religion — Islam — instead invoking belief and religious practice more generally.

Dr. El-Sayed

“My name is Abdul. It means ‘servant.’ I pray every day. I reflect on my role in this life, on this earth. How we leave it better than we found it. To serve God, to serve our neighbors.

All across Michigan, families pray. They feel hopeless. Faith is a thing there’s just too little of in Washington. We don’t have faith in our future. We don’t have faith that we can actually fix things.

So, yeah, we need a few more people of faith in Washington. I’m Abdul El-Sayed, man of faith. That’s a good thing. And I approve this message.”

Republicans have lobbed frequent attacks at Dr. El-Sayed during a bitter Senate campaign, invoking his Muslim faith, including calling him a “jihadist” and a “Muslim radical.” By leaning into that faith in his latest ad, the candidate appears to implicitly rebuke his opponents, including President Trump, who have repeatedly attacked him for it.

Dr. El-Sayed’s race against Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman, is one of the tightest of the midterms, and will most likely help determine control of Congress for Mr. Trump’s final two years in office. Dr. El-Sayed, a vocal critic of the Israeli government, squeaked out a narrow primary victory against a strong defender of the country.

Some Democrats saw that as a referendum on the party’s position on Israel, while Republican leaders used Dr. El-Sayed’s position to help fuel Islamophobic attacks that sought to portray him as an anti-American extremist.

Mr. Trump has made Dr. El-Sayed’s faith, as well as his name, a recurring theme at rallies across the country in recent weeks as he seeks to boost Republican chances. “I call him Mohammed. item.title: Trump Urges Voters to Focus on Him. Republican Ads Tell a Different Story.
item.description:
At rallies across the country, President Trump has implored voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” in the midterm elections.

But on the airwaves, his party is sending the opposite message.

Less than $1 of every $100 in Republican television ad spending on House and Senate races from Sept. 9 through Oct. 17 has gone toward commercials that mention the word “Trump,” according to a New York Times analysis of broadcast and streaming ad data and transcripts from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Mr. Trump’s approval rating is well under water, putting Republicans in a difficult spot in battleground contests that could decide control of Congress.

Note: Data includes only broadcast and streaming ads aired between Sept. 9, 2026 and Oct. 17, 2026.

Source: AdImpact

Lazaro Gamio and Bayliss Wagner

Democrats, in contrast, have spent $20 out of every $100 on spots mentioning Mr. Trump during that period, which covers much of the final sprint before Election Day. They have run heavily against the president, opposing the war with Iran, tariffs, cuts to health-care spending and the handling of the Epstein files. Many other Democratic ads do not mention Mr. Trump by name, but are critical of his policies.

The starkly divergent strategies reflect one of the defining dynamics of the final weeks of the campaign season. Republicans are increasingly trying to distance themselves from the president’s unpopular agenda, while Democrats are hoping to tie them to it.

“When the president’s approval rating is in the 30s, that’s not generally something that’s helpful for a campaign that needs to get to 50 percent of the vote,” said Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster and strategist.

The current dynamic differs sharply from the primaries, when Republican candidates, eager to appeal to the base and demonstrate their fealty to Mr. Trump, spent a much larger share of their ad dollars on commercials mentioning the president— $55 of every $100, according to the Times analysis. (AdImpact uses artificial intelligence to transcribe TV ads.)

“Voters blame what they’ve done for the pain that they’re feeling, so Republicans don’t want to own that,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “But you don’t get to start the fire and then get credit for calling 911.”

He added that Republicans “need a time machine, not an ad buy.”

Amount spent by each party on ads mentioning President Trump.

Source: AdImpact

Minho Kim and Bayliss Wagner/The New York Times

Battleground Republican Senate candidates and their allies have largely steered clear of mentioning Mr. Trump in recent ads. And when they do talk about him, it frequently comes with a catch.

Senator Dan Sullivan, the Alaska Republican running for re-election in a tight race, said in an ad released on Oct. 7 that he “voted to force Trump’s D.O.J. to release the Epstein files.”

Other Republicans have tried a more indirect strategy. Former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, sought to distance himself from Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada in an ad first aired on Oct. 10.

“Canada is not our enemy,” Mr. Rogers said in the ad. “We need to end this tariff war now. As Michigan’s senator, I’ll bring both parties together to lower your prices.”

Democrats, meanwhile, have spent most heavily on anti-Trump attack ads in states the president lost or that he won narrowly in 2024, including Maine, Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire, according to the Times analysis of AdImpact data.

In an ad run by allies of Senator Jon Ossoff, Democrat of Georgia, a woman stands at a gas pump and blames Mr. Ossoff’s Republican challenger for the spike in prices caused by the Iran war.

“Mike Collins sides with Trump and we pay,” the woman says in the ad. “We can’t afford him in the Senate.” (Mr. Collins has blamed the Biden administration’s environmental policies for higher energy prices.)

In Republican primaries, where loyalty to Mr. Trump was a major factor and candidates competed to be seen as most supportive of the president, Mr. Trump’s name showed up in more than half of all Republican broadcast and streaming ad airings. His name has appeared in just three out of every 100 ad airings for the general election, according to the analysis of AdImpact data.

Democrats also spent heavily on Trump-related ads in their primaries, which were often contests over which candidate would oppose the president most fiercely: Roughly $50 of every $100 in ad dollars in House and Senate races went to TV spots mentioning the president.

Now, both parties have modulated their approach.

In August, Josh Turek, the Democratic Senate nominee in Iowa, started airing an ad in which he vowed to work with anyone, “including President Trump,” to fix the country’s “broken immigration system” and “secure the border.” Mr. Trump won Iowa three consecutive times.

In her own pivot, his Republican opponent, Representative Ashley Hinson, announced she was running to be Mr. Trump’s “top ally in the United States Senate” last year; now, she argues she can pass legislation regardless of who is in office.

“Working across the aisle isn’t always easy,” she says in an ad mentioning Mr. Trump and Democrats, “but it’s how you get results.”

While Republican candidates have not centered Mr. Trump in their midterm ads, his administration has recently promoted him in taxpayer-funded television spots. A judge ordered last week that the ads be taken down.

We've seen evidence of some Republican candidates distancing themselves from Trump, including by scrubbing his name from their websites, criticizing his policies and, in one case, demanding that a billboard about his endorsement be taken down. This data shows how widespread that distancing is in a medium both parties rely on heavily to communicate with voters.

item.title: Supreme Court Will Not Revive Plea Deal for 9/11 Defendants
item.description:
The Supreme Court announced on Monday that it would not revive a plea deal for Khalid Shaikh Mohammed and two others accused of plotting the Sept. 11 attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people, clearing the way for the possibility that they could someday face a death penalty trial.

The decision came on a routine orders list, and it did not include any reasoning or public dissents.

The order noted that Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh did not participate in the decision making. The justices are not required to note a reason for recusal, but Justice Kavanaugh had previously served as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Washington Circuit, where he handled cases involving detainees kept at a U.S. base at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba.

Lawyers for the men accused of planning and carrying out the terrorist attacks had petitioned the Supreme Court to step in and allow a plea agreement that would resolve the case with lifetime sentences, rather than facing a trial with the possibility of the death penalty.

The plea deal had been authorized in 2024 by a senior Defense Department official. Under the terms of the deal, the government had agreed not to seek the death penalty against the men in exchange for their agreement to give up their right to appeal.

A backlash quickly followed. Within days, Defense Secretary Lloyd J. Austin III abruptly canceled the deal, putting the death penalty back on the table.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

A military judge who reviewed the case had found that the plea deals could go forward, but a federal appeals court rejected that view, upholding the defense secretary’s decision to revoke the agreements.

Lawyers for Mr. Mohammed, who has been held at the U.S. naval base at Guantánamo Bay since 2006, then filed a petition to the justices, asking them to step in. Mr. Mohammad is accused of being the mastermind who planned the Sept. 11 attacks. The two other men who appealed — Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash — are accused co-conspirators.

The lawyers for Mr. Mohammed had urged the justices to take up the case, asserting that it was of “immense national importance” and that appeals courts were in “disarray” over the procedural questions involved, adding that “the stakes of the specific case are such that this court ought to have the final word.”

Lawyers for the Trump administration had urged the justices to reject the case. In a brief, Solicitor General D. John Sauer acknowledged that the “prosecutions have been lengthy and that the families of petitioners’ victims are divided about whether the continued pursuit of the death penalty is appropriate.”

But Mr. Sauer asserted that the case implicated the interests of the whole country and argued that the appeals court had “properly corrected” what he called “egregious legal errors” by the military judge in allowing the pleas to go forward. He argued there was “no need for this court’s intervention at this juncture.”

A death penalty trial for Mr. Mohammed and others accused in the attacks is projected to last more than a year. A provisional start date has been set for June 5, 2028, but it is contingent on both sides meeting a series of deadlines beforehand. One reason it has taken so long to bring Mr. Mohammed and the others to trial is the issue of their interrogations at Guantánamo in 2007 and 2008. Lawyers for the defendants have continued to assert that the confessions obtained are too tainted by torture to be used against them at trial.

item.title: Visitor Killed by Roof Debris at Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West
item.description:
A visitor on a walking tour of a major Frank Lloyd Wright architectural property in Arizona died on Friday after he was hit by debris from its roof, local officials said.

Brother Rogério Renato Mateucci, the rector of Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná in Brazil, was touring Taliesin West in Scottsdale when strong winds ripped off part of its roofing. Brother Rogério, who was a member of the Catholic order of Marists, was struck in the head and died instantly, the Scottsdale Arizona Fire Department said in a statement.

A statement from his university said he had been hit in the head by an acrylic object.

Wind warnings had been issued across the Southwest on Friday. At the Scottsdale Airport, strong winds were reported all day, with gusts reaching as high as 32 miles per hour around 2 p.m., when Brother Rogério, 55, was struck at the famed building.

Taliesin West was built in 1937 as both a living laboratory for architectural study and a winter retreat for Mr. Wright and his students. The desert studio, nestled in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains, is a World Heritage site and a National Historic Landmark.

Mr. Wright envisioned Taliesin West as a desert utopia, comprising “low-slung buildings designed to reflect the sweeping expansiveness of the desert,” according to the foundation’s website. The structure was built largely of “desert masonry,” including local rock set in wooden form, bound by a mixture of cement and desert sand to make the buildings feel like they were an extension of the desert. (Mr. Wright lived primarily at a complex known as Taliesin in southwestern Wisconsin.)

Taliesin West is closed to the public until further notice. In a statement, the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation said it “extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones” of Brother Rogério but provided no further details about the accident.

Brother Rogério’s university in Brazil, which canceled classes on Monday, said in a statement that he was on an institutional visit to Arizona State University in Tempe as part of an international immersion program.

Taliesin West is popular with tourists, with more than 100,000 visiting annually for guided walks around the property.

Over the years, the Scottsdale complex has been altered and expanded, including the addition of a music pavilion. During Mr. Wright’s time, the roofing was made out of canvas and framed by wooden beams. But a fire in the mid-1960s burned the pavilion to the ground, and it was rebuilt. By the 1990s, the roofing system was changed from fiberglass to an acrylic exterior sheet, according to the foundation’s website.

The complex has been undergoing major renovations since 2021.

item.title: U.S. Citizen Hospitalized After Being Detained by ICE, His Family Says
item.description:
A California man whose family said he was a U.S. citizen was hospitalized in Long Beach over the weekend after an altercation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement left him pinned to the ground in handcuffs.

The encounter in Southern California on Saturday is the latest mistaken detainment as ICE arrest numbers across the country continue to rise.

It was unclear on Monday what led to the encounter, how it unfolded or whether the man was still in the hospital. But officers with the Long Beach Police Department arrived at the scene after being called in for backup by ICE, which reported that vehicles were being vandalized and that there was a person “in need of medical attention,” according to a statement from the police.

Officers then took a bleeding, handcuffed man to a nearby fire station, where they removed his handcuffs and later took him to a hospital, the statement said. The police said they were not involved in immigration enforcement and did not make any arrests at the scene.

The police declined to further comment and directed questions to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The man, Ricardo Gonzalez, was riding an e-bike when he was struck by an unmarked vehicle, according to Leslie Gonzalez, his daughter, in a post on Instagram. She said in a message to The New York Times that her father was a U.S. citizen but declined to answer more questions, citing concerns for her family’s safety. But in her post, Ms. Gonzalez wrote that her father had been “tased” and pinned to the ground. Mr. Gonzalez did not respond to an interview request.

In clips posted to social media, Mr. Gonzalez appears immobilized on his stomach by officers wearing ICE vests.

“My arm is broken, stop!” he yells, asking for medical assistance as officers handcuff him, restraining his arms behind his back.

Mr. Gonzalez is one of many U.S. citizens who have been mistakenly detained by federal immigration agents in operations that are part of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In September, agents held a U.S. citizen in suburban Chicago. The man suffered injuries to his head, neck and teeth in the confrontation. This month, ProPublica reported that hundreds of U.S. citizens have been detained by immigration officers under the current administration, inadvertently caught up in federal operations. (During President Trump’s first term, a U.S. citizen was awarded a $55,000 settlement after she was wrongfully detained by ICE.)

There has also been a recent spike in ICE arrests of people with no criminal record even as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin continues to emphasize that the agency is targeting “the worst of the worst.”

In Long Beach, videos of the encounter involving Mr. Gonzalez show a chaotic scene on a neighborhood street, with onlookers yelling at law enforcement. In other clips, a woman is shown being handcuffed by ICE officers and put in a car.

“That’s my wife, and that’s a U.S. citizen,” a man is seen yelling in one of the videos, using expletives.

Mayor Rex Richardson of Long Beach said that he had spoken to Mr. Gonzalez on Sunday but that he did not have information about the woman in the other videos.

Mr. Gonzalez had called 911 on Saturday, the mayor said, adding he did not have details about how the altercation unfolded.

By the time police officers arrived, Mr. Gonzalez was being detained, Mr. Richardson said. The mayor’s team was still gathering documentation from Saturday and working to verify what happened. His office plans to submit a complaint to D.H.S., he added.

“This is his neighborhood. He’s a father, he’s a dad,” Mr. Richardson said of Mr. Gonzalez. “The reality is, you know, that wasn’t what he expected that day. He didn’t expect that his children were going to see him cuffed and on the curb. He simply just wants his kids to be safe,” the mayor added.

On Instagram, Mr. Richardson wrote that ICE did not belong in his city and that the agency’s activities had undermined community safety.

Mr. Richardson added that his team was concerned about the timing as California begins early voting.

“No one should feel intimidated or afraid to exercise their right to vote,” he said.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Justice Dept. Charges 28 in California With Voting-Related Crimes
item.description:
Justice Department officials said on Monday that they had charged more than two dozen residents in California with violating federal voting laws, part of the Trump administration’s escalating effort to assert more control over the midterm elections.

Trent McCotter, a senior department official, said at a news conference that 28 people, all of them green card holders, or legal immigrants with residency status, had been charged. Of those, 11 had already been arrested, officials added.

The arrests ramped up the administration’s campaign against voter fraud, which so far has generated scattered cases around the country but nothing like the mass fraud that President Trump frequently claims threatens the foundations of American democracy.

Mr. McCotter held up the new arrests as evidence supporting claims the administration made last week that 20,000 people in the state are “likely noncitizens” on the state voter rolls. California officials have greeted those claims with great skepticism, accusing the Trump administration of seeking to sow doubt and meddle in an election in which voting has already started, with the deadline 15 days away.

The arrests amount to “voter intimidation and a blatant attempt to undermine trust in our midterm elections,” said Janice Hahn, a former Democratic congresswoman who now serves on the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors. She added that they were “being used to paint a picture of widespread voter fraud when we know that is not the case.”

Last week, the administration sued California and Los Angeles County, demanding that a court order local elections officials to set aside any ballots from 20,000 people the administration suspects are noncitizens on the state’s voter roll.

During the news conference, Mr. McCotter said that the arrests should “ensure integrity in elections, not undermine them.” All of the 28 people charged on Monday were on the list of 20,000 names given to California officials last week, Mr. McCotter said, adding that the administration was seeking a court order to separate any mail-in ballots those people may have submitted for the current election.

In a highly unusual letter to state elections officials last week, Mr. McCotter demanded that they not count any ballots cast by those 20,000 individuals until the state could be certain they were U.S. citizens. Otherwise, Mr. McCotter suggested, California election officials could be criminally investigated or prosecuted for aiding and abetting voter fraud. President Trump echoed Mr. McCotter’s claim on social media, vowing, “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!”

On Monday, Justice Department officials said they are seeking California’s cooperation. “Our door is open — we want to collaborate with California and now with L.A. County, as well,” Mr. McCotter said.

The county registrar did not respond to a request for comment.

The Trump administration has been engaged in a far-reaching effort to find, arrest and publicize instances of voter fraud, as the president repeatedly claims, with no evidence, that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally. In the last two months alone, the Justice Department has charged 113 people across 20 states with violations of voting laws.

Legal experts and voting officials say those figures, while larger than prior years, still reflect a tiny fraction of a percent of the total voting, and therefore are not significant enough to cause alarm about the integrity of elections or the results. The 28 people charged on Monday come in a state where 16 million people voted in the 2024 general election. Officials said that of those 28 people charged, 21 cast illegal votes in past U.S. elections.

One of those charged is Omar Alexander Munoz, a 72-year-old man from Belize who was arrested at his home in Commerce, Calif., on charges of false statements in a naturalization application and fraudulent voter registration. According to a criminal complaint, records show that Mr. Munoz, who is not a U.S. citizen, voted in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 general elections.

Mr. Munoz and his lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment.

Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, said the arrests amounted to a drop in the bucket of the 23 million people registered to vote in the state.

People committing voter fraud should be prosecuted, he added, citing a case of voter fraud brought by a local district attorney. It involved a woman in Orange County, whom he described as a Republican and who registered her dog to vote and cast ballots in her pet’s name. She pleaded guilty and was required to pay for billboards saying that voter fraud is “wrong and illegal, and you should not engage in it,” Mr. Bonta said.

Shawn Hubler contributed reporting from Los Angeles, and Laurel Rosenhall from Sacramento.

item.title: Mahmoud Khalil Appeals to Supreme Court to Halt Deportation
item.description:
Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University graduate arrested last year by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents amid campus protests, appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in an attempt to prevent his deportation.

Mr. Khalil, a legal permanent U.S. resident who is married to an American, became an early and high-profile example of President Trump’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrations on college campuses.

His case presents the justices with another test of the Trump’s administration’s aggressive efforts to deport people who are in the country both legally and illegally.

The administration has said that Mr. Khalil’s prominent role in protests at Columbia against Israel’s war in Gaza and his continued presence in the United States spreads antisemitism and is at odds with Mr. Trump’s foreign policy goals. Mr. Khalil has denounced antisemitism and said that criticism of Israel is not inherently antisemitic.

Mr. Khalil had recently gotten his master’s degree from Columbia when he was arrested in March 2025 and detained on the basis of a determination by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that his presence in the United States undercut the national interest. Mr. Rubio cited a rarely used provision of a statute that gives the secretary of state sweeping power to expel foreigners.

A district court judge found that the law cited by Mr. Rubio was most likely unconstitutional and ordered Mr. Khalil released, but the Trump administration has continued to try to deport him, resulting in a series of legal maneuvers in different courts.

Mr. Khalil’s appeal to the Supreme Court comes after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit cleared the way for him to be arrested again and potentially deported.

If the Supreme Court lets that decision stand, it will likely not end the wrangling over the legality of the administration’s moves, but it could remove one of the remaining obstacles preventing Mr. Khalil from being deported. The justices will now decide whether to hear his case, a process that could take months. If they agree to review it, they would then schedule oral arguments likely in the spring and issue an opinion by the end of the court’s term in late June or early July.

Mr. Khalil has argued that the attempt to deport him violates his free speech rights. The appeals court decision did not address that question but instead dealt with a more technical dispute over which court has the authority at this stage in the litigation to review the constitutional issues in his case.

Mr. Khalil has said that his case should be heard in federal court; the Trump administration has said the case should be heard in immigration court, which is controlled by the executive branch and overseen by the Justice Department.

Judge Michael E. Farbiarz of the District Court of New Jersey sided with Mr. Khalil and ordered him released. But a closely divided appeals court agreed with the administration and said the district court had not been the proper venue to weigh his petition for release. The matter, the court said, should have initially been addressed by an immigration court.

In their filing Monday, Mr. Khalil’s lawyers told the justices that immigration law gives the federal courts the authority to review an immigrant’s constitutional challenges to punitive and retaliatory detention.

“The federal government jailed Mr. Khalil for his speech,” one of the lawyers, Alina Das, director of N.Y.U.’s Immigrant Rights Clinic, said in a statement. She urged the Supreme Court to uphold the power of federal courts to “free people from retaliatory detention and prevent the weaponization of the immigration system to punish dissent.”

The Trump administration has separately asked the Supreme Court to review the case of Badar Khan Suri, a postdoctoral fellow at Georgetown University whom officials have accused of promoting Hamas and tried to deport. D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, has asked the justices to reverse an appeals court ruling siding with Mr. Suri.

The court could decide to consolidate the two cases, which raise similar legal questions.

Monday’s request from Mr. Khalil, a Palestinian who was born and raised in a refugee camp in Syria, comes as he has been traveling the country to promote his memoir, “No Land to Stand On.” The book recounts Mr. Khalil’s harrowing experience of being arrested in the lobby of his New York apartment building and held in a detention camp in Louisiana. Mr. Khalil was held there for months and missed the birth of his child.

His case in immigration court has continued on a separate track. In April, an immigration court affirmed that Mr. Khalil could be deported, an unusually quick decision that was also characterized by other abnormalities.

Mr. Khalil can appeal the ruling of the immigration court to the conservative U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, potentially providing another avenue to eventually seek Supreme Court review.

Jonah E. Bromwich contributed reporting.

Leanne Abraham/The New York Timess

With just two weeks to go until the midterm elections, Mr. Trump’s itinerary reflects how worried the G.O.P. is about its prospects for holding onto the House and Senate, and winning governor’s races nationwide.

Traditionally Republican strongholds have become battlegrounds this cycle. Polling in these places shows that Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries for everyday Americans — have gravely threatened the party’s fortunes.

The president started his barnstorm in Kansas, with plans to pass through the Carolinas, Florida, Iowa and Georgia. He will stump in five House districts he won in 2024 by more than 20 points, and for the most part in states with unusually competitive Senate races.

Notably, he is staying away from traditional battleground states such as Maine and New Hampshire, where Republican candidates have distanced themselves from the president in hopes of winning over more moderate voters. His choice appears to signal a political strategy that focuses not on persuading swing voters but on shoring up support from the base that powered his rise.

“He goes where the battles are,” said John McLaughlin, a longtime pollster for Mr. Trump. “And this is where the battles are.”

In a more favorable political environment for Republicans, the party would be looking to pick up a seat in Georgia and defend one in North Carolina, in addition to using the president to defend its Senate seat in Maine.

But Mr. Trump and his political team have all but given up on the first two states, and have accepted the president’s inability to help Senator Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent in Maine, two advisers to the president said in interviews. This cycle, the White House sees Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Michigan as the battlegrounds, they said. Michigan represents the rare setting this year for a competitive race for a seat held by a Democrat.

“This idea that he’s going to red states, well yeah that’s where the races are right now, which tells you all you need to know,” one of the advisers said. “But also we’re playing to a national audience in terms of motivating Republicans.”

The swing will also allow Mr. Trump’s political operation to generate good “pictures” to use in advertisements beyond his actual itinerary, the adviser said.

“We play to visuals,” the adviser said. “And if we’re in a congressional district that’s next door to a competitive congressional district, what difference does it make? It’s all the same people, it’s all the same media.”

Mr. Trump remains his party’s most effective motivator a decade after he descended a golden escalator at his namesake building in midtown Manhattan to announce his first bid for the White House. Yet his popularity has dipped to historic lows, with about 37 percent of Americans approving of how he is handling his job.

The Republican National Committee, in announcing his travel, said the itinerary is intended to shore up the party’s vulnerable candidates. But the president is also known to go where he will find adoring crowds, and the midterm blitz through ruby red America provides him ample opportunity for that experience.

Mr. Trump will start the week in a House district in Wichita, Kansas, that backed him over former Vice President Kamala Harris two years ago by more than 23 points. He will then travel to Greenville, North Carolina, which, under the state’s new congressional map, would have broken for him by 14 points, before swinging through Clemson, South Carolina, to a district that he carried by a whopping 43 points. Mr. Trump will end the week with stops in deep-red Sioux City, Iowa, and Fort Myers, Florida, before a final rally Saturday in Macon, Georgia.

Next week, he will rally in Lubbock and Waco, Texas, said Republican National Committee Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre.

Vice President JD Vance, who has also embarked on a campaign swing this month, has taken a similar approach. He kicked off the week in North Carolina, and will end it in a district in Nebraska that backed the president by more than 50 points.

Kevin Madden, a Republican strategist who worked for the campaigns of former President George W. Bush and Mitt Romney, called the White House’s posture “defensive.”

“Two of the most valuable assets on any campaign are money and time,” Mr. Madden said. “Where you are spending your money and where you are spending your time in the last two weeks says a lot about your strategy.”

It isn’t just the last two weeks. This fall, the president has campaigned in the southeast corner of Oklahoma, the reddest part of one of the reddest states in the country, and swung through Western Nebraska, Northern Kentucky and Mobile, Ala., the latter being where he held his first presidential campaign in 2015 and began building his vaunted MAGA base after drawing some 30,000 to an open-air football stadium.

Nebraska and Kansas should be slam dunks for his party, even in years when Democrats do well. His Friday night visit to Dalton, Ga., was perhaps most symbolic of the party’s dire view of its position: The city sits in the heart of a congressional district once represented by Marjorie Taylor Greene, the longtime Trump ally who broke with him over the Epstein files and the war in Iran.

The approach relies on motivating less reliable voters whom Mr. Trump has shown a singular ability to motivate. At rallies over the past month, he has pleaded with them to pretend he is on the ballot. So far, the results have been mixed.

At Mr. Trump’s rally last week in Youngstown, Ohio, entire sections of the arena remained empty. But some voters who had watched from home said the event had given them more confidence in Senator Jon Husted, the Republican of Ohio in a tough race to retain his seat against Sherrod Brown, the Democrat.

“What Husted said at the rally,” said Steve Zawilinsky, a pastor who watched the rally on TV, “that is what I wanted to hear.”

Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

item.title: Manchin Says He Will Campaign With Collins in Maine
item.description:
Former Senator Joe Manchin III of West Virginia, a longtime centrist Democrat who became an independent shortly before he retired last year, plans to campaign in Maine this week for Senator Susan Collins, a Republican seeking her sixth term.

In an interview, Mr. Manchin said he wanted to join Ms. Collins because he had “never” worked with a “more centrist, independent-minded person.” He said he expected to spend all day Wednesday with her in Androscoggin County, in southwestern Maine, which voted for President Trump in the last three presidential elections.

Ms. Collins is in a tough re-election fight with her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, a logger from northern Maine who morphed from Republican to progressive Democrat across a long political career. Over the last few months, and especially across the candidates’ four debates, Mr. Jackson tried to hammer Ms. Collins’s connection with President Trump, while she focused on portraying herself as an independent voice who crossed party lines several times to vote in the Senate.

Mr. Manchin scoffed at Mr. Jackson’s claims that Ms. Collins had been a rubber stamp for President Trump. “She’s not Donald Trump’s senator,” Mr. Manchin said. “She’s not the Republican senator. She’s Maine’s senator.”

Mr. Manchin said on CNBC last month that he would be campaigning for Ms. Collins, but he had been speaking with her for a long time about actually going to Maine.

“I said, ‘Whenever you run again, I’m going to come. I’ll be there if you want me to,’” Mr. Manchin said, adding, “You lose Susan Collins, you lose the soul of the Senate.”

item.title: Man Who Died in ICE Custody Was Denied Medicine, His Daughter Says
item.description:
When Estefani Andrade spoke over video last Friday to her father, who was in an immigration detention center in Texas, he looked pale and unwell, she said. The next day, he was found unconscious in his cell, and she was later told he died.

The man, Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, who had a heart condition, diabetes and high blood pressure, had complained to his daughter for months about the lack of medical care at the Rio Grande Processing Center, a detention center in the border city of Laredo, Ms. Andrade said.

“He was coughing. He didn’t look like himself,” Ms. Andrade said. “I asked if she was OK. He said, ‘they don’t listen to me.’”

“We want to know why this had to happen,” she added.

The death of Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias, 56, was confirmed Monday by Henry Cuellar, a Democratic member of the U.S. House who represents Laredo and was briefed on the matter by immigration officials.

Ms. Andrade said her father was given medications to treat his illnesses only during his first weeks in detention. She said her father complained that he could not receive additional medicine until it was approved by a doctor.

But ICE said in a statement that Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias had received “proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.”

“He had a documented medical history of diabetes, hypertension, and anxiety,” ICE added.

Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias’s death has raised more questions about the medical care provided at the detention centers in Laredo and around the country.

Since President Trump returned to office, immigrants and activists have described haphazard health care and poor conditions at detention centers run by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The number of immigrants deaths in ICE custody has nearly doubled under the Trump administration.

Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias is the second detained migrant to die in similar circumstances at an immigration detention center in Laredo this year. ICE had said that Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, 63, of Mexico, was found unresponsive on June 19 while detained at the Webb County Detention Center, which is also in Laredo. He was later pronounced dead at a hospital.

Mr. Cuellar said in an interview Monday that Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias, who had been detained since June, was found unresponsive at around 10 a.m. on Saturday during a security check inside his cell. The staff at the detention center performed CPR and called 911, Mr. Cuellar said. An autopsy report is pending, Mr. Cuellar said.

The Rio Grande Processing Center is operated by a private company called the GEO Group, which referred questions to ICE.

Mr. Cuellar also said that the legal status of Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias was unclear. Immigration officials described him to Mr. Cuellar as a “citizen of Mexico,” he said. But in conversations with the man’s family and Mexican consulate officials, Mr. Cuellar was told that the man was a legal U.S. resident.

“We need to have transparency,” Mr. Cuellar added. “We need to get information as quickly as possible.”

ICE said it had determined that Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias had obtained legal status “through fraudulent means” because he failed to disclose his prior arrest during the review process. He was in the process of being removed before an immigration judge when he died, ICE said.

Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias left Hidalgo, Mexico, as a teenager and settled in the Dallas area, Ms. Andrade said. He lived there for decades and had three children. He had been a U.S. legal resident for about 10 years and often traveled to Mexico and had no problem traveling to and from the United States as a legal resident, she added.

That changed in June, when he was detained coming back from Mexico by bus, she said.

Ms. Andrade said she believed that her father’s detention stemmed from an arrest more than two decades ago. In 2004, Mr. Andrade-Covarrubias, who painted apartments and townhouses, stole a ladder as payment from a client who Ms. Andrade said had refused to pay him for his work. He was arrested, but it was unclear he if was convicted in the case.

On Monday, his daughter was given his belongings and was trying to console her mother and two younger brothers.

“I have to be the strong one,” she said. “We have so many questions. He is not the only one to die like this.”

item.title: U.N.C. Strikes Trump Deal to Keep Federal Funding
item.description:
The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and the federal government said on Monday that they had reached a settlement to close 19 federal inquiries. The agreement made U.N.C. the latest school to align itself formally with the Trump administration’s vision for higher education.

The university, which did not acknowledge wrongdoing, will not pay any money in connection with the agreement, setting it apart from schools that pledged to shell out tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. But it agreed to abide by the Trump administration’s views on matters like admissions; diversity, equity and inclusion; and the punishment of student groups for actions perceived as antisemitic.

In return, according to U.N.C. and the Justice Department, the university preserved its access to federal research funding — crucial for a school that draws most of its research money from Washington. The government also said it would not use the agreement to control “academic speech or curricula” at U.N.C., long regarded as one of the nation’s top public institutions.

And the government agreed to shut down 18 investigations by the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights, as well as a compliance review the Justice Department opened last year. According to U.N.C., the investigations concerned matters like antisemitic harassment and sex and race discrimination.

Lee H. Roberts, U.N.C.’s chancellor, said in a statement that the settlement “reinforces our commitment to the fair and equal treatment of everyone at Carolina.”

The Justice Department, which has put legal pressure on schools from coast to coast, seized on the agreement to argue that other universities should curtail their fights against a government that many in academia believe is suppressing dissent and debate.

“Higher-ed policies and practices that tolerate antisemitism or favor certain racial groups over others, frustrate our colorblind justice system,” Harmeet K. Dhillon, the Justice Department’s top civil rights official, said in a statement. “The Civil Rights Division commends U.N.C. for its cooperation in meeting its obligations under federal law without the need for litigation; we hope other institutions will take note and do the same.”

The settlement comes a little more than three years after U.N.C., along with Harvard, lost before the Supreme Court when the justices rejected the schools’ affirmative action programs. Monday’s agreement puts significant attention on admissions — a recent focus of the Justice Department — at U.N.C.

The university agreed, for example, that it would not “by any means, including considerations of racial diversity, preference applicants in admissions based on any protected characteristic.” The university also promised to “not allow or tolerate, and shall actively eliminate, the use of racial proxies as a means of preferring applicants for admission on the basis of race or other protected characteristic.”

In recent years, students and faculty members at U.N.C. have blistered the university for embracing some conservative priorities, such as a civic life school. The university system as a whole has moved to stamp out D.E.I. programs, and Mr. Roberts, a former state budget director under a Republican governor, has been repeatedly criticized for his reluctance to challenge a White House that has openly threatened elite higher education. Mr. Roberts has denied any partisan motivations for his strategy, and he was among the university leaders who rebuffed a government proposal last year that dangled preferential treatment for research funding in exchange for ideological fealty.

Few people at the university had known that it had been in talks with the government.

Devin Duncan, the student body president and an ex officio member of the campus’s board of trustees, said in an interview on Monday night that he believed there were a “fair number of people who are concerned” after the announcement. The worry, he said, was not only a “slippery slope” with a Trump administration that has reveled in punishing top schools, but also the precedent that the agreement could set for U.N.C.’s dealings with future presidents.

“There is legitimate concern about what does this mean?” said Mr. Duncan, a junior. “Does it open the door to political influence?”

But he still welcomed the relief, for now, in research funding.

The Trump administration has reached settlements with a handful of other top schools, including Brown, Columbia, Cornell and Northwestern. But the U.N.C. agreement may be most similar to ones the government signed with the University of Pennsylvania and the University of Virginia, which also inked policy-driven settlements that included no financial penalties.

Noel T. Brewer, a professor in U.N.C.’s public health school, expressed skepticism about the endurance of the administration’s agreements with universities.

“These settlements between the universities and the current administration appear to be politically expedient and existential,” he said in a text message.

U.N.C.’s agreement expires on Dec. 31, 2028 — weeks before President Trump is scheduled to leave office.
